opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question, and I think for me it didn't come from one single moment. It built up over time, through experiences and through watching the people around me.

Part of it is simply growing up and noticing that opportunities aren't distributed evenly. Some people get encouragement, resources, and the benefit of the doubt, and others have to work twice as hard just to be taken seriously. Once you start seeing that, you can't really unsee it. I've been lucky to have mentors and collaborators who believed in me and gave me room to try things. That made me realize how much difference one person's support can make, and it made me want to be that person for others.

Working in computer science, and especially in AI systems research, has also shaped how I think about it. The field is still not very diverse, and you notice who is in the room and who isn't. I don't think that's because talent is unevenly distributed. It's because access, networks, and confidence are. So I care a lot about open source and open research. When you make tools, models, and knowledge freely available, a student anywhere in the world can pick them up, learn, contribute, and build something meaningful. To me that's one of the most practical forms of fairness: lowering the barrier so that what matters is your ideas and effort, not where you come from.

And finally, I think fairness is something you have to practice in small, everyday ways: how you credit people's work, how you listen in meetings, who you invite to collaborate, how you treat a newcomer asking a basic question. Big principles matter, but they really show up in those small choices. That's what I try to hold myself to.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think it really comes down to lived experience more than any single moment. I grew up in a context where the path forward was supposed to look a certain way, and I was often one of very few women in the room, whether that was in math competitions, in my PhD program, or later working on systems research. You start to notice who gets invited to speak, whose ideas get credited, who gets the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong. Those small things add up, and once you see them, you can't unsee them.

The other piece is open source. Working on projects like SGLang, where anyone can contribute regardless of where they're from or what institution they belong to, taught me a lot about what fairness can actually look like in practice. The best contributions I've seen came from people I would never have met otherwise, sometimes students in places with far fewer resources than Berkeley or a big lab. That made the case for me very concretely: when you lower the barriers, you don't lower the quality. You raise it, because you're drawing from a much bigger pool of talent.

And honestly, being an immigrant shapes it too. You experience firsthand how much of your opportunity depends on policies and gatekeepers you had no part in choosing. That makes you want to build things, and communities, where the door is open a little wider for the next person.

astra-6.text: For me, it starts with the belief that everyone deserves dignity and a fair chance. When you think about how much someone’s opportunities can depend on circumstances they didn’t choose, it’s hard to see fairness as just an abstract principle. It becomes a question of whose voice gets heard, whose potential gets recognized, and who gets left out. I think that commitment also means being willing to listen and reconsider your own assumptions, because you can care about equality and still miss barriers that other people face.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it starts with the belief that everyone deserves dignity and a fair chance. It’s easy to say we value equality, but the harder question is whether people actually have the same opportunity to be heard, to participate, and to succeed. Equal treatment doesn’t always mean equal access, so fairness also means paying attention to the barriers people face. I think that commitment requires listening, questioning our assumptions, and being willing to change how we do things.
